title: The 2030 Legal Department: 5 Ways AI Will Transform How In-House Teams Work
pub: Thomson Reuters / Thomson Reuters Institute (GCO 2030 programme)
author: Norie Campbell · Lizzy Duffy

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Buyer transformation: Legal departments may capture AI gains
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core proposition that in-house AI gains depend on organisational absorption and service-delivery redesign, not individual tool adoption or cost cutting alone. It materially extends that proposition with concrete operating archetypes for workflow automation, augmented advice, business self-service and global collaboration, plus specific requirements around data infrastructure, coordination, skills and process redesign. Its contribution is primarily a forward-looking implementation framework rather than evidence of realised transformation outcomes.
qs: We understood that closing this gap would require redesigning end-to-end workflows so that the system as a whole is faster, not just the individuals within it.

**Efficiency is a by-product of transformation, not the whole story.** The important question is not how to do current work better, but what kind of legal function your organization needs in 2030 — and what it would take to build it.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: The source strongly accepts the cluster’s operating-model proposition and materially develops it for in-house departments through a flexible archetype framework and specific implementation priorities across workflows, data, coordination, skills and technology. It also reinforces the cluster’s caution that current gains are incremental and transformation remains provisional rather than demonstrated at scale.
qs: We understood that closing this gap would require redesigning end-to-end workflows so that the system as a whole is faster, not just the individuals within it.

From that process, three insights emerged: a need to redesign how work flows through our team; recognition that data infrastructure is our single biggest structural constraint; and an understanding that, while individual practice areas need flexibility, we could supercharge our efforts with intentional GCO-level coordination.

st.t: Value capture: Integrated delivery reshapes market boundaries
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core proposition that AI value depends on redesigning integrated legal delivery rather than merely accelerating individual tasks. It materially extends that proposition from the in-house perspective by identifying data infrastructure and GCO-level coordination as structural requirements and by recommending capability assessment, multidisciplinary hiring and process simplification before tool deployment. Its conclusions remain provisional and grounded in its own planning exercise rather than market-wide outcomes.
qs: We understood that closing this gap would require redesigning end-to-end workflows so that the system as a whole is faster, not just the individuals within it.

From that process, three insights emerged: a need to redesign how work flows through our team; recognition that data infrastructure is our single biggest structural constraint; and an understanding that, while individual practice areas need flexibility, we could supercharge our efforts with intentional GCO-level coordination.

st.an: The source strongly accepts the cluster’s proposition that task-level AI gains do not by themselves create organisational value. It materially extends that position with an in-house transformation framework centred on end-to-end workflow redesign, data infrastructure, maturity assessment and GCO-level coordination, while treating deployment paths as organisation-specific rather than prescriptive.

From that process, three insights emerged: a need to redesign how work flows through our team; recognition that data infrastructure is our single biggest structural constraint; and an understanding that, while individual practice areas need flexibility, we could supercharge our efforts with intentional GCO-level coordination.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s emphasis on workflow and organisational reconfiguration rather than simple labour replacement or isolated efficiency gains. Its department-specific, strategic framework aligns with the need for organisational complements and selective redesign, though it does not substantively address verification, competence or apprenticeship risks and remains forward-looking rather than empirical.
qs: Every legal department is different, and the right transformation path will depend on the nature of the work, the structure of the organization, and the ambitions of the team.

kp.k: Efficiency alone understates AI’s transformational potential
kp.d: The authors argue that faster and cheaper execution of existing legal tasks is only an incremental use of AI. Their GCO 2030 framework instead asks how AI could redesign the legal department’s capabilities, workflows, relationships, and strategic role by 2030; it is presented as a vision and framework, not a proven roadmap.
qs: The obvious answer about efficiency — faster contracts, cheaper research, fewer repetitive tasks — only describes what AI can do for the work a legal department already does, not what a legal department could become.
The goal is not to offer a roadmap but a framework to help move from the pressure to "do something with AI" to a clear, considered answer to the harder question.
Efficiency is a by-product of transformation, not the whole story.

kp.k: Cost pressure precedes demonstrated AI value
kp.d: Interviews with senior in-house leaders in early 2026 identified persistent pressure on general counsel to do more with less. The authors report concern among those leaders that executives may invoke AI to justify reducing legal-department headcount before AI’s practical value has been established.
qs: The most consistent pressure facing GCs today is the expectation to do more with less.

That finding emerged across interviews Thomson Reuters Institute conducted with senior in-house leaders in early 2026, along with a growing concern that executive leadership is using AI as justification for headcount reduction before its practical value has been demonstrated.
As technology evolves faster than teams can absorb, many are caught between the risk of falling behind and the fear of moving too fast.

kp.k: AI should multiply capabilities, not merely reduce costs
kp.d: The authors argue that treating AI solely as a cost-cutting mechanism will forgo opportunities to improve lawyers’ capabilities and redesign departmental work. They connect this opportunity to the expanding strategic remit of general counsel amid geopolitical, regulatory, and global business complexity.
qs: Add to this the ever-broadening advisory remit of the GC to act as a strategic advisor to businesses facing geopolitical uncertainty, regulatory flux, and the increasing complexity of doing business globally.
Organizations that treat AI only as a cost-reduction mechanism rather than a capability multiplier will miss out.
The departments that move forward with a clear sense of what they want to become and why will have the chance to redesign how they work for the better.

kp.k: Individual adoption does not produce systemic transformation
kp.d: Every organization interviewed had some AI activity, but Thomson Reuters’ own GCO found that widespread personal use and several material proof points yielded only incremental efficiency. The authors conclude that transformation requires systematic deployment and end-to-end workflow redesign rather than faster individual task performance.
qs: Every organization we spoke to had at least some AI activity underway, ranging from informal pilots to structured deployment programs.
But adoption is not the same as transformation — and our own GCO was stuck in the adoption phase.
However, what this was delivering was only incremental efficiency gains that wouldn’t be sufficient to meet our ambitions or the needs of the business.
We understood that closing this gap would require redesigning end-to-end workflows so that the system as a whole is faster, not just the individuals within it.

kp.k: Five archetypes frame alternative transformation paths
kp.d: The source proposes five interconnected but non-exclusive models: Scaled Enablement, Advisory Plus, Empowering Peer, Seamless Integrator, and Global Leverage. The appropriate combination is said to depend on work type, opportunity scale, organizational structure, ambitions, and AI readiness; Thomson Reuters’ approximately 80-lawyer, multi-practice, multi-geography GCO expects to combine models.
qs: To help legal departments — including our own — move forward with clarity, we have developed five distinct archetypes for the AI-transformed legal department.
The archetypes are not mutually exclusive.

For large, full-service legal departments like the Thomson Reuters GCO — with approximately 80 lawyers across multiple practice areas and geographies — the right answer is likely a combination, deliberately chosen for each team based on factors such as its work type, the scale of the opportunity, and AI readiness.
For smaller departments, one or two archetypes may provide the clearest focus.

kp.k: Scaled Enablement automates high-volume routine legal work
kp.d: Scaled Enablement targets contract review, routine compliance checks, standard-form processing, and intake triage—high-volume tasks requiring relatively little legal judgment. The authors describe this as the likely entry point and foundation for other transformations because manually processing routine volume constrains lawyers’ capacity for strategic work.
qs: Scaled Enablement means transforming high-volume, repetitive work through AI-powered automation.

The goal is to handle the tasks that occupy significant time but require relatively little legal judgment, including contract review, routine compliance checks, standard-form processing, and intake triage.
This archetype is the most likely entry point for many departments because it addresses the most universal constraint — work volume.
A legal team that is still handling high-volume, routine tasks manually does not have the capacity to become a strategic advisor, a better partner to the business, or a genuinely global function.

kp.d: The authors warn against automating existing complexity, which they call an efficiency trap. Their recommendation is to simplify and redesign processes before deploying tools so that AI removes bottlenecks and frees legal expertise for higher-value matters rather than reproducing inefficient workflows.
qs: The key to success here is to avoid simply automating existing processes, as this leads to the efficiency trap.

Investing time in simplifying and redesigning processes first pays off by freeing up the legal team’s capacity and expertise to focus on more strategic, higher-value matters and by removing the bottlenecks in current systems.
Process redesign before tool deployment to build on simplified workflows rather than automating complexity

kp.k: Advisory Plus augments rather than replaces judgment
kp.d: Under Advisory Plus, AI performs substantial data analysis, precedent research, and drafting while lawyers retain legal judgment. The predicted effect is faster, better-informed advice and greater capacity for the legal department to engage early as a strategic business partner, rather than merely reducing lawyer numbers.
qs: Advisory Plus means having AI do the heavy lifting on data analysis, precedent research, and document drafting — not to replace legal judgment, but to make it better informed, faster, and more efficiently deployed.
It is not the last stop in a process, but a proactive partner to the business, one that engages early and contributes genuine strategic counsel.
Removing the administrative weight and adding the AI “superpower” changes what lawyers can do, not just how many of them you need.

kp.k: Empowering Peer embeds legal guidance across business functions
kp.d: The Empowering Peer model uses AI-enabled tools, playbooks, guardrails, and workflows to let procurement, HR, finance, sales, and other functions handle routine legal-adjacent work themselves. The authors predict that legal input can thereby be delivered earlier and at greater scale without removing the legal department from governance.
qs: The Empowering Peer archetype inverts that dynamic.

Powered by AI, legal actively improves other functions' work by building tools, playbooks, guardrails, and embedded workflows that allow finance, HR, procurement, sales, and others to handle routine legal-adjacent work themselves, with confidence and at speed.
Legal is not removed from the picture; it is present in a different and more powerful way, embedded in how other functions operate rather than sitting at the end of a queue.
Legal's value is delivered earlier, more consistently, and at a greater scale than the traditional advisory model could achieve.

kp.k: Integration standardizes internal and external legal delivery
kp.d: The Seamless Integrator model addresses duplicated effort and uncertainty over whether law firms share AI efficiencies. It proposes common playbooks, quality standards, and AI-powered review and grading for internal lawyers, outside counsel, ALSPs, and managed service providers, making quality measurable and enabling coordinated allocation of work across providers.
qs: Clients don’t know whether efficiency gains from AI are being shared.

In-house counsel is too often doubling up with external counsel on a file to guide the risk-reward decision, to translate advice to internal stakeholders, and to explain how the business processes really work.

The Seamless Integrator archetype addresses this duplicity by building the infrastructure — like consistent playbooks, shared quality standards, and AI-powered review and grading — that makes outside counsel relationships genuinely strategic rather than transactional, enabling seamless toggling between internal and external teams.
This archetype also extends to alternative legal service providers (ALSPs) and managed service providers.

kp.k: AI may reduce global language and timezone inequalities
kp.d: The Global Leverage archetype predicts that translation, multilingual drafting and review, collaboration tools, and asynchronous workflows can reduce structural disadvantages affecting lawyers outside English-language and core-time-zone hubs. The supporting account includes a reported GC example from an organization operating across 21 countries, but the broader effects remain prospective.
qs: One GC at an organization operating across 21 countries was candid about the reality that time differences, language, and the need to fully contribute in an English-language environment pose real barriers.

Global Leverage is the archetype that uses AI to remove these barriers — not just through translation in the literal sense, but with the full range of tools that enable a lawyer in any location, in any language, to contribute at the same level as their colleagues in London or New York.
That full range includes auto-translation in collaboration tools, AI-powered drafting and review in multiple languages, and asynchronous workflows that do not privilege a single time zone.
This archetype can elevate a legal team to a truly global function, drawing on the full range of its talent, unconstrained by geography or first language.

kp.k: Data infrastructure is the principal structural constraint
kp.d: Thomson Reuters’ internal maturity assessment found a gap between widespread individual AI use and desired systematic deployment. Mapping transformation across people, process, data, and technology led the GCO to identify data infrastructure as its single largest structural constraint, alongside workflow redesign and a need for coordinated department-level action.
qs: Our first step was to understand the current AI maturity levels across the GCO.
We found a gap between where the teams were, which was widespread individual use of AI tools, and where they wanted to be, which was systematic deployment.
Next, we mapped teams’ transformation visions across people, process, data, and technology.

From that process, three insights emerged: a need to redesign how work flows through our team; recognition that data infrastructure is our single biggest structural constraint; and an understanding that, while individual practice areas need flexibility, we could supercharge our efforts with intentional GCO-level coordination.

kp.k: Future lawyers require technical and workflow capabilities
kp.d: The authors recommend capability-based AI training and hiring lawyers who combine legal expertise with technical literacy, workflow-design ability, and adaptability quotient. They also treat legal operations capacity as a prerequisite for transformation and urge lawyers to conceptualize work as workflows rather than isolated tasks.
qs: AI training and upskilling grounded in a genuine assessment of current capability rather than assumption
Hiring toward the profile of the future lawyer, with technical literacy and workflow-design capability alongside legal expertise and adaptability quotient (AQ)

Assess AI capability honestly rather than optimistically, build legal operations capacity as a prerequisite rather than an afterthought, and hire or develop lawyers who think about their work in terms of workflows rather than tasks.

kp.k: Strategic archetypes require slower-building organizational foundations
kp.d: The authors state that Scaled Enablement generally offers the quickest, most visible results, while Advisory Plus and Empowering Peer tend to promise greater strategic value. Those more ambitious models depend on data, redesigned workflows, capacity, and cross-functional trust, so quick wins should support rather than displace longer-term transformation.
qs: Start with quick wins, but don’t lose sight of the bigger transformation.
Scaled Enablement tends to produce the fastest and most visible results, but the archetypes that tend to generate the most strategic value are Advisory Plus and Empowered Peer.
However, they require foundations such as data, workflow redesign, and cross-functional trust that take longer to build.

kp.k: Human and AI task boundaries remain unsettled
kp.d: The authors qualify their 2030 vision by acknowledging uneven implementation, sustained organizational effort, and uncertainty over which tasks will continue to require human judgment. Because technology, markets, and the profession remain in flux, they recommend building an adaptable, technically capable legal organization rather than attempting to specify a fixed endpoint.
qs: The gap between aspiration and operational reality takes real work and long-term commitment to close.

While we have a working hypothesis for the future role of the lawyer in a genuinely AI-powered team, the line between work that requires human judgment and skills and the repetitive, rule-based tasks moving to AI is shifting.
The archetypes and the journey we have described are not a prescription.
The 2030 legal department isn’t a destination you can design in full detail today, because the technology, the market, and the profession are still evolving.
What you can do is build an organization with the capacity to adapt — curious, technically capable, and clear about the value it is trying to deliver.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Campbell and Duffy predict that AI can transform corporate legal departments through five complementary operating models, going beyond individual efficiency gains to change capacity, strategic advice, business self-service, external-provider coordination, and global participation.
pts.d: The authors present these models as their GCO 2030 vision, not as established outcomes. (1) Scaled Enablement: AI automation of high-volume, relatively low-judgment work, including contract review, routine compliance checks, standard forms, and intake triage, can free lawyers for higher-value matters. Simplifying and redesigning processes first is central to the claimed benefit. They expect this model to be the most common entry point and to produce the fastest, most visible results. (2) Advisory Plus: AI-assisted analysis, precedent research, and drafting can make human legal judgment better informed and faster, while removing administrative burdens lets lawyers engage earlier as strategic advisers. This is augmentation, explicitly not replacement of legal judgment. (3) Empowering Peer: legal-designed AI tools, playbooks, guardrails, and embedded workflows can let procurement, HR, finance, and sales handle routine legal-adjacent work themselves. The authors predict faster procurement and sales, better employment decisions, and less waiting for compliance assistance, without a lawyer participating in every negotiation. (4) Seamless Integrator: shared playbooks, quality standards, and AI-powered review and grading can reduce duplication between internal and external counsel, make work quality visible and comparable, and enable more coordinated allocation across law firms, ALSPs, and managed service providers. AI review and grading here concern evaluation of legal work, rather than a reported model benchmark or a human-verification protocol. (5) Global Leverage: multilingual drafting and review, automatic translation, and asynchronous workflows can reduce language and time-zone disadvantages and enable lawyers outside central hubs to contribute more equally; 'leverage' here denotes global capability, not an associate-to-partner staffing ratio. Beyond the archetypes, the authors report that strong individual AI adoption in their own GCO has produced only incremental gains and argue that end-to-end workflow transformation is necessary. They foresee a changing division between human-judgment work and repetitive, rule-based work moving to AI, and identify technical literacy, workflow-design capability, adaptability, and legal operations capacity as increasingly important. Interviewed senior in-house leaders report concern that executives are using AI to justify headcount reductions before its practical value is demonstrated; the article does not establish actual reductions or forecast their magnitude.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is qualitative interviews and the authors’ early experience assessing and planning transformation within Thomson Reuters’ own GCO; the five archetypes are a proposed framework rather than quantitatively demonstrated results.
pts.d: Campbell, Thomson Reuters’ chief legal officer, and Duffy, a senior director at the Thomson Reuters Institute, draw on Institute interviews with senior in-house leaders conducted in early 2026. They report consistent pressure to do more with less, concern about premature AI-based headcount rationales, and at least some AI activity in every organization interviewed. The article supplies no interview sample size, sampling method, or quantitative adoption or headcount results. An unnamed GC describes the aspiration to make strategic advice an operational reality; another, at an organization operating in 21 countries, describes language and time-zone barriers. These interview observations support the problems the models seek to address, rather than demonstrate their predicted benefits. The internal experience concerns a GCO of approximately 80 lawyers across practice areas and geographies. The authors report above-average individual adoption, live proof points, an AI-maturity assessment, and mapping of team visions across people, process, data, and technology. They identify fragmented individual use, workflow redesign needs, and data infrastructure as constraints. They do not specify the comparison underlying 'above average', describe the proof points in detail, or provide measured time savings, quality improvements, cost reductions, or comparative outcome evidence for the archetypes. The claimed relative speed and strategic value of different models are the authors’ observations and expectations, not benchmark findings.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The article, dated May 28, 2026, sets a 2030 planning horizon, with early-2026 observations and immediate foundational actions; transformation is conditional, organization-specific, and not presented as a guaranteed endpoint.
pts.d: GCO 2030 launched in early 2026. Its archetypes describe what corporate legal functions could become by 2030, without year-by-year targets or quantified implementation timelines. The authors say daily AI use must build habits, infrastructure, and confidence, but individual adoption alone is insufficient. Scaled Enablement requires process simplification and redesign rather than automation of existing complexity. Advisory Plus and Empowering Peer are expected to yield the most strategic value, but depend on slower-to-build data foundations, redesigned workflows, and cross-functional trust. Seamless Integrator depends on consistent playbooks, shared quality standards, and infrastructure for commissioning and assessing work across providers. Global Leverage depends on multilingual tools and workflows that do not privilege one time zone. The appropriate mix varies by work type, opportunity, AI readiness, organizational structure, and ambition: large full-service departments may combine models, while smaller departments may focus on one or two. Immediate actions include assessing skills, training, hiring or developing technically literate and workflow-oriented lawyers, building legal operations capacity, and redesigning processes before deploying tools. The authors acknowledge uneven team progress, long-term commitment, a shifting human–AI task boundary, and continuing changes in technology and the market. Their own experience is expressly not a universal prescription.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected group is corporate in-house legal teams, with consequences for business colleagues, external legal-service providers, geographically dispersed lawyers, and legal hiring and operations.
pts.d: GCs and CLOs face pressure to expand strategic advice while controlling resources, including reported executive expectations about AI-related staffing reductions. In-house lawyers are expected to spend less time on routine work and more on judgment, earlier business engagement, and workflow design. Legal operations capacity becomes a prerequisite for sustained transformation. Future hires and existing lawyers are expected to need technical literacy and adaptability alongside legal expertise. Procurement, HR, finance, and sales gain guarded self-service for routine legal-adjacent tasks, while legal expertise becomes embedded in their processes. Law firms, ALSPs, and managed service providers would face common quality standards and more integrated commissioning and assessment by corporate buyers; the article does not predict provider market shares or a particular pricing model. Lawyers working outside English-language environments or central time zones are expected to gain more equal opportunities to contribute. Large multinational and full-service departments may deploy multiple archetypes, whereas smaller departments may pursue a narrower combination. The claimed benefits concern enterprise capability and service delivery, not access to justice for underserved individuals or measured public outcomes.
